w: Opened in 1911, this hotel has anchored central Surabaya for over a century. It is now part of Accor's boutique MGallery collection -- one of the city's oldest hotels still welcoming guests, elegance intact through a hundred years of change.
s: The city's oldest grand hotel, open since 1911
_facts: Historic hotel in Surabaya opened in 1911
Currently managed by Accor through its MGallery chain

w: The oldest mosque in East Java, raised in 1421 by Sunan Ampel, one of the saints credited with spreading Islam across the island. His tomb sits within the same complex, still drawing pilgrims today, folded into Surabaya's oldest quarter.
s: East Java's oldest mosque, built in 1421
_facts: Ancient mosque in Ampel sub-district, Semampir, Surabaya
Oldest mosque in East Java, built 1421 CE by Sunan Ampel
Sunan Ampel's tomb complex is located within the area

w: An evangelical megachurch on a scale that is hard to picture: weekly attendance was clocked at 140,000 in 2020, run by a father-to-son pastoral succession. One of the largest single congregations anywhere, tucked into an ordinary Surabaya suburb.
s: A megachurch drawing 140,000 worshippers a week
_facts: Evangelical megachurch affiliated with Bethany Indonesian Church
Senior pastor David Aswin Tanuseputra since 2012, succeeding his father
2020 attendance recorded at 140,000 people

w: A Dutch colonial compound built in 1862 as an orphanage, bought in 1932 by Sampoerna founder Liem Seeng Tee to hand-roll the country's cigarettes. Restored for the firm's 90th anniversary, it now mixes a tobacco museum with a cafe and gallery -- though it has been shut since the pandemic.
s: A colonial orphanage turned tobacco museum
_facts: Dutch colonial-style compound built 1862, formerly an orphanage
Purchased 1932 by Liem Seeng Tee, founder of Sampoerna, as first cigarette factory
Restored for 90th anniversary in 2003; museum, cafe and gallery
Closed to the public since the COVID-19 pandemic

w: A Chinese temple inside a seaside amusement park, watched over by a 20-metre Guan Yin statue at the water's edge. The story goes a temple worker once saw a woman in white walking on the sea at closing time -- taken as the goddess herself, and the reason the statue was built.
s: Seaside Chinese temple watched over by Guan Yin
_facts: Chinese temple in Pantai Ria amusement park, Surabaya
20-metre statue of Guan Yin on the waterfront
Legend: an employee saw a woman in white walking on the sea, taken as Guan Yin's appearance
Also has a giant gold-covered Phra Phrom statue

w: A 60-metre bronze naval officer stands guard over the Port of Tanjung Perak, sword at his side, eyes fixed on the horizon as if daring the tide itself. Built to embody the Indonesian Navy's readiness, it is one of the tallest figurative statues in the country.
s: A 60-metre bronze sailor guarding the harbour
_facts: Statue of an Indonesian Navy officer near the Port of Tanjung Perak
Stands 60.6 metres tall
Represents the Indonesian Navy's preparedness

w: Housed in the old De Javasche Bank building, the Dutch colonial-era central bank that kept functioning as a Bank Indonesia branch until 1973. Restored and reopened as a museum in 2012, it traces the country's currency and banking history -- and it is free to walk in.
s: Free museum inside the old colonial central bank
_facts: Occupies the former De Javasche Bank building, Dutch East Indies central bank
Functioned as Bank Indonesia's branch until 1973
Opened as a museum 27 January 2012 after restoration
No entrance fee; closed Mondays and public holidays

n: Church of the Birth of Our Lady, Surabaya
w: Known locally as Kepanjen Church, this is Surabaya's oldest Roman Catholic parish, completed in 1899 and still standing in the old quarter. A quiet holdover from the Dutch colonial era, predating most of the city built up around it.
_facts: Also known as Kepanjen Church
Roman Catholic church completed 1899
Oldest Roman Catholic church in Surabaya

w: More than five thousand war dead lie here -- Dutch colonial soldiers and civilians from the Pacific War and Indonesia's fight for independence. At the centre stands a monument to Karel Doorman, the naval commander lost at the Battle of the Java Sea, its bronze plates naming 915 men never recovered.
s: Resting place for over 5,000 war dead
_facts: Over 5,000 victims of the Pacific War and Indonesian War of Independence buried here
Monument to naval officer Karel Doorman at the centre
Commemorates the Battle of the Java Sea, 27 February 1942, 918 Dutch sailors killed
Names of 915 missing on fifteen bronze plates

w: Indonesia's second-largest mosque, its 99-metre minaret counting off the names of Allah and its half-egg dome unlike any other in the country. Construction stalled for two years when the 1997 financial crisis hit, before President Abdurrahman Wahid inaugurated it in 2000.
_facts: Second largest mosque in Indonesia after Istiqlal Mosque, Jakarta
Minaret 99 metres tall, referencing the 99 names of Allah
Groundbreaking 1995; construction suspended by 1997 Asian financial crisis
Completed 2000, inaugurated by President Abdurrahman Wahid

w: A mosque built like a Chinese temple, pagoda roofline and all, raised inside the compound of Surabaya's Chinese Muslim association just north of downtown. The city's tourism board promotes it as a stop for religious tourism -- proof that faith and heritage can share a roofline.
s: A mosque built like a Chinese temple
_facts: Mosque with Chinese architectural influences in Ketabang, Genteng, Surabaya
Located within the Indonesian Chinese Muslim Association (PITI) complex
Promoted by Surabaya Tourism Board as a religious tourism site
